question: Is quantum mechanics complete?
denyLabel: Incomplete — not yet the real thing
context: Born and Heisenberg's joint report ended by calling quantum mechanics a closed theory. Einstein, who declined to give a report, used the general discussion to question whether ψ could be a complete description of an individual process.
later: EPR (1935) turned the question into an argument; Bell (1964) turned it into an experiment. The experiments rule out local completions; nonlocal completions such as Bohm's (1952) remain logically possible.

question: Is probability fundamental?
context: Born's 1926 collision papers introduced the probability interpretation. Einstein had used transition probabilities since 1916 but regarded them as provisional.
later: No experiment has found structure beneath quantum probabilities that restores local determinism. Whether the probabilities are fundamental remains an interpretive question: pilot-wave and many-worlds theories are deterministic at the level of their equations.

text: The wave function represents physical reality.
question: What does the wave function describe?
affirmLabel: A real wave in the world
denyLabel: A tool for probabilities or knowledge
context: Schrödinger read ψψ* as a density of charge; de Broglie treated the wave as a real guiding field; Born read |ψ|² as a probability; Heisenberg treated it as a summary of possible observations.
later: Still disputed. So-called ψ-ontic and ψ-epistemic views were sharpened in the 2010s (for example by the Pusey–Barrett–Rudolph theorem, 2012), but no consensus exists.

text: Additional quantities, beyond ψ, may restore determinism.
question: Could further quantities restore determinism?
affirmLabel: Yes — ψ is not the whole state
context: De Broglie presented a pilot-wave dynamics at this council. Einstein had quietly withdrawn his own attempt in May 1927. The phrase 'hidden variables' is later; in 1927 people spoke of quantities that would determine the individual process.
later: Von Neumann's 1932 'proof' was taken to settle the matter until Bell (1966) showed its key assumption unwarranted. Bohm's 1952 theory showed a deterministic completion is possible — but Bell's theorem shows it must be nonlocal.

question: Does measurement require an observer?
context: Heisenberg wrote that the path comes into existence only when observed. In the general discussion Dirac said nature makes a choice; Heisenberg replied that the observer makes it. Bohr spoke of the whole experimental arrangement, not of minds.
later: Decoherence (from 1970) explains why interference disappears once a system is coupled to an environment, without invoking minds — though it does not by itself explain why one outcome occurs.

text: The electron has definite properties before measurement.
question: Does the electron have properties before it is measured?
affirmLabel: Yes — values exist to be found
context: The uncertainty relations were published in March 1927. The question of whether they limit knowledge or limit reality was open in the room.
later: Bell-type experiments and the Kochen–Specker theorem (1967) show that assigning all values in advance, independently of the measurement context and locally, is impossible. Nonlocal, contextual assignments (as in pilot-wave theory) survive.

question: Are quantum jumps real?
context: In October 1926 Bohr pressed Schrödinger on this for days in Copenhagen. Schrödinger hoped continuous wave processes would replace jumps.
later: Single-atom experiments from 1986 observed jumps directly in the fluorescence of trapped ions; in 2019 experiments at Yale caught a jump in progress and reversed it — a continuous, predictable process on short timescales.

text: Physics must provide pictures in space and time.
question: Must physics give us pictures?
affirmLabel: Yes — or it is not yet physics
denyLabel: No — the formalism is the physics
context: Anschaulichkeit was a charged word in 1926–27. Schrödinger claimed it for wave mechanics; Heisenberg redefined it in his uncertainty paper.
later: Modern physics largely accepted abstract formalisms, but pictures returned in new forms: Feynman diagrams, phase-space pictures, and visualisable pilot-wave trajectories measured as averages in 2011.

text: Light and matter are both waves and particles.
question: Are light and matter both waves and particles?
context: The council was titled Électrons et Photons. Compton's effect (1923) and electron diffraction (1927) had made both halves of the duality experimental facts.
later: Quantum field theory treats both as excitations of fields. Single-photon and single-electron interference, and interference of large molecules, are now routine.

text: The law of causality fails in atomic processes.
question: Does causality fail in the atom?
context: Heisenberg's uncertainty paper ended by declaring the final failure of causality. Lorentz, Planck and Einstein resisted.
later: The debate shifted from 'causality' to 'determinism' and 'locality'. Relativistic causality — no signalling faster than light — survives in quantum theory.

text: Physics should speak only of observable quantities.
question: Should physics speak only of what can be observed?
context: Heisenberg's 1925 paper was built on observable quantities. Einstein, who had once used a similar principle, told him in 1926 that theory decides what can be observed.
later: Modern theory is full of unobservable structure — quarks confined inside hadrons, gauge fields — justified by its observable consequences.

text: No influence can act instantaneously at a distance.
question: Can there be action at a distance?
context: In the general discussion Einstein argued that if ψ completely describes one electron, its localisation on a screen would imply a peculiar action at a distance.
later: Bell's theorem and loophole-free experiments (2015) show that no local theory reproduces the observed correlations. Quantum theory still forbids faster-than-light signalling.
